source.title_on_document: Groups and AI: How Access to Generative AI Influences Creative Teamwork

supplement.where: The paper mentions no online supplement. Appendix A (user creations, pp. 415-420) and Appendix B (Figure 4, Study 1 questionnaire ratings, p. 421) are part of this PDF.
supplement.holds: Nothing outside this PDF. No means, SDs, or standard errors are printed for any rating of the outputs. Study 2 results are F statistics, p thresholds, and post-hoc statements in Section 4.1 (p. 410); rating levels appear only as bars with SD whiskers in Figure 2 (p. 411).

paper_design_summary: In Study 1, six groups of three (18 people analyzed, no exclusions reported), recruited by convenience sampling in a university context, each did two roughly 20-minute marketing-campaign tasks for a fictitious product (name, slogan, 2-3 selling points, and a pen-and-paper sketch of product and logo), once with ChatGPT-4o and once with Google search only, with the order of conditions and products counterbalanced, not stated as randomized. Participants rated their own group's result and process, and sessions were video-coded. In Study 2, 20 external online raters, blind to AI use, rated the 12 resulting campaigns on six Creative Product Semantic Scale items and ranked the six results of each campaign.

studies.label: Study 1 lab experiment (six groups of three, ChatGPT-4o vs Google search, within-group crossover), with the outputs rated by the paper's Study 2 external raters

assignment.what_was_assigned: Access to ChatGPT-4o (AI) versus the Google search engine without AI functionality (No AI). Every group did both conditions, one per product (Glowing Umbrella, Smart Plant Pot). The order of conditions and products was counterbalanced, not stated as randomized. Appendix A shows the pairing: Glowing Umbrella with AI for groups 01 and 04 and without AI for groups 02, 03, 05, 06; Smart Plant Pot the other way round.
assignment.quote: The order of conditions and products was counterbalanced across 6 trials, ensuring that each combination was used once.

arms.name: AI
arms.description: ChatGPT-4o displayed on a shared 55-inch screen, with one mouse and keyboard, for the whole group during the roughly 20-minute campaign task.

arms.name: No AI
arms.description: No AI tools; the Google search engine without AI functionality on the same shared screen during the roughly 20-minute campaign task.

participants.exclusions: None reported. 18 people took part in six groups of three, and all 18 are analyzed. Every person took part in both conditions, so each arm holds the same 18 people (6 groups). The final-questionnaire counts each sum to 18 (preference: 7 AI, 4 No AI, 7 no clear preference; perceived AI role: 12 guide, 5 teammate, 1 leader; p. 410, Section 4.1), and all 12 group results (6 groups x 2 conditions) appear in Appendix A and were rated in Study 2. The 20 Study 2 raters are a measurement panel, not participants who received AI help.
participants.who: Convenience sample in a university context: 9 male, 9 female, aged 20 to 29 (mean 25.6, SD 2.7); computer science the most common professional background, with many STEM fields; all had used AI tools before (7 daily, 5 weekly, 6 less than weekly); not compensated. The paper does not state whether participants were students.
participants.country: not_stated (authors at RWTH Aachen University, Germany; study conducted in English)
participants.quote: 18 people (9 male, 9 female) aged 20 to 29 years (mean = 25.6, SD = 2.7) participated in Study 1.
participants.locator: p. 409, Section 3.1; p. 413, Section 8 (Conclusion, 'six groups of three')

ai_tool.how_used: Free use by the whole group on a shared screen; participants were not forced to use it. All groups used it to produce text (the paper's examples are product names and slogans), and most groups generated at least five images per session, then tried to transfer the last image to their hand drawing (p. 410, Section 4.2.1; p. 412, Section 4.2.3; p. 413, Section 5).

task.description: Ideate a marketing campaign for a fictitious product (Glow-in-the-dark Umbrella or Smart Plant Pot) on a structured worksheet: name the product, create a slogan, give 2-3 core selling points, and sketch the product and a logo with pen and paper.
task.duration: Each condition designed to take approximately 20 minutes (p. 409, Section 3.1)

outcomes.name: External rating: Conventional/Original (Creative Product Semantic Scale item)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Paper's Study 2: 20 external online raters (7 male, 13 female, aged 18 to 53; 13 with a technical and 3 with a creative background), blind to AI use, rated all 12 Study 1 results (6 per campaign) on this item, plotted from -2 (left property) to 2 (right property); campaign and result order randomized. Analysis: non-parametric ANOVA based on Aligned Rank Transform with factors Use of AI and Campaign, and Holm-corrected Wilcoxon signed-rank post-hoc tests. The unit of analysis and the number of ratings are not stated.

contrasts.reported: No significant effect reported for originality. Section 4.1 reports Study 2 effects only for Organized, Practicability, Appeal, and focus, and the introduction says the externals' creativity ratings 'did not show an overall tendency for GenAI assisted results'. Figure 2 (Study 2 panel): AI bar slightly longer than No AI bar, with SD whiskers; no numbers printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 408, Section 1; p. 410, Section 4.1; p. 411, Figure 2

outcomes.name: External rating: Predictable/Unexpected (Creative Product Semantic Scale item)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same 20 external raters, scale, and analysis as S1-O1.

contrasts.reported: No significant effect reported. Figure 2 (Study 2 panel): AI and No AI bars nearly equal, with SD whiskers; no numbers printed.

outcomes.name: External rating: Disorganized/Organized (Creative Product Semantic Scale item)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same 20 external raters, scale, and analysis as S1-O1; how organized the campaign result is.

contrasts.reported: Effect of Use of AI F1,57=5.43, p ≤ 0.05; interaction of Campaign and Use of AI F1,57=20.45, p ≤ 0.001. Post-hoc (Holm-corrected Wilcoxon): Smart Plant Pot×AI significantly more organized than Smart Plant Pot×No AI and Glowing Umbrella×AI (p ≤ 0.05). The direction of the main effect comes from Figure 2 (AI bar longer) and the introduction ('significantly more organized ... for one of the tasks').

outcomes.question: with_ai

outcomes.name: External preference ranking of the six results per campaign
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Paper's Study 2: after rating, each of the 20 external raters ranked the 6 results of each campaign 'on their preference' (rank 1 = best). Figure 3 plots how often AI and No AI results received each rank (axis 0 to 120 rankings per condition). No test reported.

contrasts.reported: 'AI results were ranked slightly better.' (Figure 3 caption); 'Overall, the AI results were rated and ranked slightly better than the No AI results.' No test and no numbers printed.

outcomes.name: Self-ratings of own group's result on the six Creative Product Semantic Scale items (Study 1 participants)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: After each condition, Study 1 participants rated their own group's result on originality, organization, practicability, predictability, appeal, and definition, plotted from -2 to 2; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Self-rated creativity by the creators, so it does not meet criterion 3.

contrasts.reported: 'Using the GenAI tool did not lead to any significant differences in the self-reported creativity ratings for our participants.' The only significant Study 1 questionnaire effect was on cognitive effort (Z = -3.18, p ≤ 0.01), a process measure. Item levels appear only as bars in Figure 2 (Study 1 panel); no test statistics are printed for these items.
contrasts.locator: p. 408, Section 1; p. 410, Section 4.1; p. 411, Figure 2; p. 412, Section 5

outcomes.name: Self-reported preference between the two campaigns and which condition's results felt more creative (Study 1 final questionnaire)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Final questionnaire: which campaign each participant preferred, with written justifications, and whether the group's results felt more creative with or without AI. Self-report, so it does not meet criterion 3. Preference favors AI and perceived creativity favors No AI, hence direction mixed.

contrasts.reported: '7 participants preferred AI, 4 No AI, while the remaining 7 had no clear preference.' 'Most of the participants felt like the group produced more creative results when using No AI, while only 4 felt that their AI-assisted results were more creative.' No test reported.

company_involvement.description: No company involvement stated. The work was funded in part by the German B-IT Foundation.

eligibility.reason: Within-group lab experiment: six groups of three (18 people analyzed, no exclusions reported) each worked once with ChatGPT-4o and once with Google search, with the order of conditions and products counterbalanced and not stated as randomized (criterion 1 unclear; p. 409, Section 3.1). The 18 people analyzed are far below 50. The 20 Study 2 raters scored the outputs and received no AI help, so they do not count (criterion 2 not met). Blind external ratings of the group outputs meet criterion 3 (p. 409, Section 3.2). Core is no under any answer to criterion 1, because criterion 2 fails. The paper goes to the screening report as an experiment with fewer than 50 participants whose randomization is not stated.

one_line_finding: With six groups of three (18 people analyzed), 20 blind external raters rated ChatGPT-assisted marketing campaigns more organized (F1,57=5.43, p ≤ 0.05) and more well-defined (F1,57=4.38, p ≤ 0.05) than Google-search campaigns, with post-hoc AI-versus-No-AI differences only for the Smart Plant Pot; the paper reports no significant effect on originality or unexpectedness, the raters ranked AI results slightly better (no test), and participants' self-ratings showed no significant differences (p. 408, Section 1; p. 410, Section 4.1; p. 411, Figures 2-3).
open_questions: Counterbalancing: the text says the order was 'counterbalanced across 6 trials, ensuring that each combination was used once', but Appendix A pairs the Glowing Umbrella with AI in 2 groups (01, 04) and without AI in 4 (02, 03, 05, 06), and the Smart Plant Pot the other way round, so the product-condition pairing is unbalanced. The order of conditions per group is not reported, and the paper does not say whether groups were allocated to sequences at random.

Unit of the Study 2 analysis: not stated. The residual df of 57 is consistent with one score per rater per Use of AI x Campaign cell (20 raters x 4 cells), but the paper does not say so, and it does not print the number of ratings per item. Assignment was by group, so the independent units are the 6 groups (each in both arms); the paper's tests treat raters as the units (codebook Section 10).
Population: the paper does not say whether the university convenience sample were students; population is coded mixed provisionally.
Whether a counterbalanced crossover whose order is not stated as randomized satisfies criterion 1; moot here because criterion 2 fails.
notes: The paper's Study 2 is an online rating study of Study 1's outputs. It assigned nothing and has no arms, so its ratings are recorded as outcomes of S1 (S1-O1 to S1-O7), not as a separate study. Rater sample: 20 people (7 male, 13 female) aged 18 to 53 (mean = 27.55, SD = 8.09), 13 with a technical and 3 with a creative background (pp. 409-410, Section 3.2). Outputs are group-level: 12 campaign results (6 groups x 2 conditions), shown in Appendix A (pp. 415-420). Not listed as outcomes because they are not scored on the output: NASA-TLX cognitive effort (AI mean = -0.56, SD = 0.78 vs No AI mean = 0.33, SD = 0.84; Z = -3.18, p ≤ 0.01; p. 410), the other NASA-TLX, Team Effectiveness, and own process items (Figure 4, p. 421), the perceived role of AI (12 guide, 5 teammate, 1 leader; p. 410), and video-coded collaboration behaviors from reflexive thematic analysis (pp. 410-412). No diversity or homogenization outcome. Figures 2, 3, and 4 are vector graphics in the PDF, so bar ends, SD whiskers, and the Figure 3 rank frequencies can be read exactly from the drawing coordinates at extraction; the paper prints none of these values. Outcome IDs follow screener A; screener B's S1-O3 (Practical) and S1-O4 (Organized) are S1-O4 and S1-O3 here. open_items.item: Allocation of the six groups to condition order (open questions 1 and 4). The paper says the order of conditions and products was 'counterbalanced across 6 trials, ensuring that each combination was used once' (p. 409, Section 3.1), but Appendix A pairs the Glowing Umbrella with AI in 2 groups (01, 04) and without AI in 4 (02, 03, 05, 06) (pp. 415-420), the order of conditions per group is not reported, and the paper never says whether groups were allocated to sequences at random. Under the codebook, a within-person design meets criterion 1 only when the order of conditions is randomized: criterion 1 is met if the authors confirm random allocation and not met if allocation was systematic (the design class would then be quasi_people, not lab_rct). Core stays no under either answer, because the 18 people analyzed fail criterion 2. The PDF is the version of record, with no supplement and no posted data, so only the authors can settle it.

Unit of the Study 2 analysis (open question 2). The paper does not say whether the Aligned Rank Transform ANOVA used single ratings or one score per rater and cell, and it prints no number of ratings; the residual df of 57 fits 20 raters x 4 Use of AI x Campaign cells (p. 410, Section 4.1). Criterion 3 is met under any unit, because blind external raters scored the outputs. The unit matters only for the standard-error basis of a pooled estimate (codebook Section 10), and this paper stays out of the dataset.

Population code (open question 3 and the one unresolved reconciliation difference). The paper describes a convenience sample 'in a university context' (p. 409, Section 3.1) and 'comparably young adults with a technical and academic background' (p. 413, Section 6), but never says whether they were students, so population stays mixed provisionally. It affects no criterion.
